papers.title: Deep Cross-Division Network for Product-and-Ratio Feature Interactions in Industrial Ranking
papers.authors: Sofia Gulevskaia, Maksim Utushkin, Aleksandr Poslavsky, Alexander D' Mikhail Trapeznikov, yakonov
papers.abstract: Learning effective feature interactions is essential for industrial recommender systems. DCN and DCNv2 efficiently automate polynomial feature crossing. However, their cross layers construct interactions using only non-negative integer powers of the input features, with the maximum degree controlled by network depth. Consequently, they cannot directly represent the reciprocal terms required for ratios, rates, and normalized counts unless such features are explicitly provided as inputs. We introduce DCDN, a Deep Cross-Division Network that augments a DCNv2-style cross layer with a division branch. DCDN jointly learns product, ratio, and mixed product-ratio interactions. We characterize the representable interactions as multivariate Laurent polynomials and show that a $K$-layer DCDN generates Laurent monomials of $\ell_1$-order up to $K+1$, with signed degree between $-K$ and $K+1$. We evaluate DCDN against a production-optimized neural-ranking baseline built around DCNv2 and supplied with manually engineered ratio features. Replacing the DCNv2 block with DCDN allowed us to eliminate the entire class of manually engineered ratio features from the model input, reducing the number of input features by $40.1\%$. DCDN is deployed in the production ranking stack of a major short-video service. In a live A/B test on this service, DCDN increased likes by $3.25\%$, shares by $16.26\%$, total view time (TVT) by $0.33\%$, and clicks to open fullscreen by $0.38\%$; all changes were statistically significant. The number of shown videos decreased slightly ($-0.24\%$). These results demonstrate that DCDN can improve user engagement while eliminating reliance on manually engineered ratio features. Our code is publicly released at this https URL.
papers.summary: Industrial rankers often have to engineer ratio features such as click-through rates by hand, because DCNv2-style cross layers only form polynomial products and cannot represent reciprocal terms directly. Adding a division branch to the cross layer lets the model learn both product and ratio interactions from the same base features, so the entire class of hand-built ratio features can be dropped from the input. In the production ranking stack of a major short-video service, that cut the number of input features by 40.1%. In a live A/B test, likes rose 3.25% and shares rose 16.26%, both statistically significant, while the number of shown videos dipped only slightly. ==Ratios no longer have to be stacked into the input by hand, because the interaction layer can learn the normalized relationships itself==, and model computation time fell as well.

papers.title: Beyond Covers and Titles: Evidence-First Ranking for Robust Cold-Start Recommendation
papers.authors: Fuyi Wang, Yuxin Cao, Yifan Liao, Renyang Liu, Lin Li, Wei Song
papers.abstract: Short-video platforms rank new uploads before anyone has watched them, using content towers that read a video's cover, title and frames. Existing attacks on content-aware recommenders perturb pixels or features and ignore platform re-encoding, and existing defenses train against norm-bounded perturbations that neither match real edits nor preserve recommendation quality. We show with REAP, a realizable attack through {a simulated platform channel (H.264 transcoding, rescaling, cropping and JPEG)}, that packaging edits raise a cold video by 32.0 rank-percentile points in unrelated audiences. We then observe that cold-start ranking does not need the packaging at all: a tower that sees only the video body ranks cold items best. Building on this, we propose Evidence-First Ranking (EFR), which scores cold videos from their body, admits packaging only through a support-gated residual bounded by $\gamma$, and merges cold and warm rankings by rank percentile, yielding an exact certificate against any packaging edit. On MicroLens-100K, EFR cuts the attack gain by 81% and raises cold-start Recall@100 from 0.1133 to 0.170, while keeping the merged NDCG@10 within 4% of the undefended system.
papers.summary: Short-video platforms rank new uploads from covers, titles, and frames before anyone has watched them, so creators can buy exposure by editing that packaging. After transcoding, rescaling, and compression, such edits can raise a cold video by 32.0 rank-percentile points among unrelated audiences on a SigLIP content tower. Cold-start ranking does not actually need the packaging: a model that sees only the video body ranks cold items better. The new ranker scores cold videos from the body, admits packaging only through a bounded residual, and merges cold and warm lists by rank percentile, which yields a certificate against any packaging edit. On MicroLens-100K, that cuts the attack gain by 81%, while the merged NDCG@10 stays within 4% of the undefended system. ==What proves the content is the video body, so covers and titles should not dominate cold-start exposure==.

scenario: Today's personalization track asks what a production ranker should trust: engineered features, or the content itself. On one side, industrial ranking has long relied on hand-built ratio features because cross layers can form products but not divisions; after a division branch is added, a short-video production stack drops about two-fifths of its input features and still lifts likes and shares online. On the other, cold-start ranking still reads covers and titles, and those packaging edits can raise a cold video among unrelated viewers even after transcoding. Scoring cold items from the video body and admitting packaging only through a bounded residual cuts most of the attack gain, with little loss in the quality of the merged list. Taken together, today's question is how to fold recurring ratio structure into the model, and how to tell which signals actually prove the content.
